content: The first quantitative measurement of the speed of light was conducted in 1676 by Ole Christensen Rømer. He utilized a telescope to study the orbital motions of Io, one of Jupiter's moons. Rømer observed that Io's orbital revolution could be timed because it regularly entered and exited Jupiter's shadow. When Earth was closest to Jupiter, the timing of Io's shadow exit was consistent. However, as Earth and Jupiter moved farther apart, the observed exit of Io from Jupiter's shadow occurred progressively later than predicted. This delay was attributed to the additional time required for light to traverse the increasing distance between the two planets. Conversely, when Earth and Jupiter approached each other, the timing of Io's shadow exit became earlier than expected. Based on these observations, Rømer estimated that light would take approximately 22 minutes to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit (twice the astronomical unit). Modern calculations place this time at about 16 minutes and 40 seconds. At the time, the astronomical unit was estimated to be approximately 140 million kilometers. Christiaan Huygens combined Rømer's time estimate with the astronomical unit to calculate the speed of light as 1,000 Earth diameters per minute, equivalent to about 220,000 kilometers per second. This value was 26% lower than the currently accepted speed of light but still significantly faster than any known physical phenomenon of the era. Isaac Newton also accepted the finite speed of light, estimating it at 210,000 kilometers per second (6 Earth diameters per second), which was 30% less than the actual value. It is unclear whether Newton derived this estimate from Rømer's data or other sources. Rømer later observed the same effect with a rotating spot on Jupiter's surface and with the other three Galilean moons, although these observations were more challenging. These findings helped address objections to the concept of a finite speed of light. While not universally accepted at the time (notably by Jean-Dominique Cassini), the hypothesis of infinite light speed was largely discredited after James Bradley's observations in 1728. Bradley deduced that starlight falling on Earth would appear to come from a slight angle due to the Earth's motion in its orbit relative to the speed of light. This phenomenon, known as the aberration of light, was measured to be about 1/200 of a degree. Using this effect, Bradley calculated the speed of light to be approximately 298,000 kilometers per second (185,000 miles per second), which is less than 1% below the currently accepted value. The aberration effect has been extensively studied in subsequent centuries, notably by Friedrich Georg Wilhelm Struve and Magnus Nyren. The first successful terrestrial measurement of the speed of light was conducted by Hippolyte Fizeau in 1849. Fizeau's experiment involved directing a beam of light at a mirror several kilometers away. The light passed through a rotating cogwheel on its way to the mirror and back. At a specific rotation speed, the light beam could pass through one gap in the cogwheel on its outward journey and another gap on its return. At slightly different rotation speeds, the beam would strike a tooth of the cogwheel and fail to pass through. By knowing the distance to the mirror, the number of teeth on the cogwheel, and the rotation rate, Fizeau calculated the speed of light to be 313,000 kilometers per second. His method was later refined by Marie Alfred Cornu in 1872 and Joseph Perrotin in 1900. Leon Foucault improved upon Fizeau's method in 1862 by replacing the cogwheel with a rotating mirror. Foucault's estimate of the speed of light was 298,000 kilometers per second, a value that closely aligns with the currently accepted figure. Foucault's method was subsequently used by Simon Newcomb and Albert A. Michelson. Michelson, in particular, dedicated much of his career to refining these measurements. In 1926, Michelson employed a rotating prism to measure the time it took for light to travel a round trip between Mount Wilson and Mount San Antonio in California, a distance of approximately 36 kilometers (22 miles). His precise measurements yielded a speed of 299,796 kilometers per second (186,285 miles per second). During World War II, advancements in radar technology and the development of cavity resonance wavemeters enabled laboratory-based measurements of the speed of light. C. Gordon-Smith used a microwave cavity with precisely known dimensions to determine the frequency of various normal modes of microwaves, which, like all electromagnetic radiation, travel at the speed of light in a vacuum. By combining the known wavelengths of these modes (derived from the cavity's geometry and electromagnetic theory) with their associated frequencies, the speed of light was calculated. The result, 299,792 ± 3 kilometers per second, was significantly higher than values obtained using optical techniques, sparking considerable debate. This value was later refined to 299,792.5 ± 1 kilometers per second and was adopted by the 12th General Assembly of the Radio-Scientific Union in 1957. Most subsequent measurements have been consistent with this value. With modern electronics, particularly oscilloscopes capable of sub-nanosecond time resolution, the speed of light can now be directly measured by timing the delay of a light pulse from a laser or LED as it reflects off a mirror. Such experiments are now routine in undergraduate physics laboratories.
